 Follow Air Traffic Control Scolded Downed Learjet Over ‘Severe Turbulence’ Months Before Crash
 Brian Particelli Wed, November 4, 2026 at 8:28 PM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Meteorologist Dylan Federico Facebook The Learjet that tragically crashed in Palm Beach, Florida was involved in another instance of "severe turbulence" months before it went down.
 Audio obtained by the Daily Mail from May 2026 begins with an air traffic controller asking a female pilot why the jet was climbing in altitude.
 "We are just about to call you, we are experiencing moderate chop and unable to hold altitude," she responded, before the controller told her, "That's not moderate. Descend to 4,000 [feet] immediately ."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement After she said they were descending, a male pilot was heard reiterating that they were experiencing "moderate chop." The controller, however, insisted, "If you can't maintain altitude that is not moderate, that is severe turbulence."
 He then asked, "Are you experiencing severe turbulence?" before both pilots responded, "Affirmative, sir."
 While the Daily Mail confirmed the Learjet being flown at the time had the same tail number as the one that crashed, the outlet was unable to confirm who was flying the jet at the time.
 X/prolific369; The Palm Beach Post
 As In Touch previously reported, Captain Jeffrey Gregory , 55, and copilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras , 20, were in the cockpit when the aircraft went down on Sunday, November 1, while en route to the Bahamas.
 Advertisement Advertisement NTSB's Tom Chapman told reporters, per ABC News , that ice and turbulence were "certainly a factor" in the crash, which claimed the lives of a pilot, copilot, and seven passengers. He also said, according to Fox News Digital , that "weather conditions" were a "major focus" of the investigation, as the jet flew through a powerful thunderstorm.
 Per the NTSB, Filgueiras requested permission to climb to 37,000 feet after the jet began to experience turbulence and ice while flying at 35,000 feet. Less than 30 seconds after air traffic control approved the request, the aircraft began its sudden descent, before it crashed, killing all nine aboard.
 Adam Robinson , his wife, Helen Sharp , their children — Emma , 2, and Charlie , 4 — as well as the children's nanny, Anita Maria Apellido Cetina , were among the passengers who perished . Another couple, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr , also died.
 The cause of the crash remains under investigation.
